anchors.quote: the first thing and it always stands out is the formatting

claim_en: When a CV opens, the first thing the recruiter notices, and it always stands out, is the formatting.

anchors.quote: I think managers don't like seeing too many colors They prefer very streamlined easy to read CV So such as bold um underlined titles when it comes to jobs

claim_en: The recruiter thinks managers do not like seeing too many colors and prefer a very streamlined, easy to read CV, such as bold or underlined job titles.

anchors.quote: And then obviously companies people I've worked at those are like that is the first thing that I see

claim_en: The companies the candidate has worked at are among the first things the recruiter sees.

anchors.quote: the second thing is obviously looking at uh job titles
obviously the job titles can be different so that's perfectly fine someone might call someone else might call themselves a front end engineer that's okay

claim_en: The second thing the recruiter looks at is the job titles; titles can differ for the same kind of work, which is perfectly fine.

anchors.quote: pick out certain technologies Make sure the technologies match

claim_en: If the titles look good, the recruiter picks out the technologies and makes sure they match the role.

anchors.quote: Make sure if it's a front end technology job it's not backend technology I'm seeing everywhere no front end because that obviously rules it out quite quickly

claim_en: For a frontend job, a CV with backend technology everywhere and no frontend is rejected quite quickly.

anchors.quote: to go even deeper after that is to see the sort of impact the contributions they've had um the achievements the statistics uh for example of how much they reduce crash rates

claim_en: Going deeper, the recruiter looks for the impact, the candidate's contributions and achievements, and statistics such as how much crash rates were reduced.

anchors.quote: Me as an external recruiter it's my job to help people fix CVS as well So I do not judge someone fully on that

claim_en: As an external recruiter, the recruiter helps candidates fix their CVs and does not judge someone fully on the CV.

anchors.quote: if it's a financial firm I'm looking for fintech finance experience stuff like that as well depending on what the manager has told me

claim_en: Depending on what the hiring manager has said, the recruiter looks for industry experience, such as fintech or finance experience for a financial firm.

anchors.quote: I'm not a fan of AI CVs and managers do pick on it very very quickly
They're they're using AI day-to-day but they don't also want to see too much AI uh in CVS

claim_en: The recruiter is not a fan of AI-written CVs; managers pick up on them very quickly and, although they use AI day to day, do not want to see too much AI in CVs.

anchors.quote: I don't think there there is a problem with it as long as you then go back and change things around

claim_en: Using AI to write the CV is not a problem as long as the candidate then goes back and changes things around.

anchors.quote: There are managers who say to me I actually want to open up the like have AI in your like live coding

claim_en: Some managers tell the recruiter they want candidates to use AI in live coding, to see how they work with it and how much they rely on it.

anchors.quote: the manager said to me if if you if I look at a CV and I know you could have written it as an out when I don't do engineering then it means that you know it's not it's not enough
they want to know okay but what have you actually built to how has that changed the business
you know the statistics you know the individual contribution you had

claim_en: A manager told the recruiter that a CV of standard content that a non-engineer could have written is not good enough; managers want to know what the candidate actually built, how it changed the business, the statistics and the individual contribution.

anchors.quote: No no I actually do it all manually
there is a feature on LinkedIn where you can actually go back and filter them by how many of the keywords they have I don't really really do that
We don't run ATS Um our clients do but myself personally no I I have to look through it myself

claim_en: In the recruiter's own agency every application is screened by hand: the agency runs no ATS (its clients do), and the recruiter does not use LinkedIn's keyword filter.

anchors.quote: A lot of the applications we send is on LinkedIn send it or on a job board and it goes into an ATS system um an application tracking system which managers CCVs on and then it goes through AI what score and everything else right and then it gets lost sometimes in there
Sorry this was the AI that said no I actually want to interview you

claim_en: Applications sent on LinkedIn or a job board go into the employer's ATS, where AI scores them and they sometimes get lost; managers have told candidates it was the AI that said no.

anchors.quote: I don't think you need to always write up for every bullet point because some bullet points are obviously a lot quicker

claim_en: Not every bullet point needs the full problem, action and impact write-up; some bullet points are a lot quicker.

anchors.quote: what we tell people to do is between that job title and the bullet point have a paragraph
didn't explain this company is this and this It works in this sector I worked with this amount of people Some of the biggest problems we face is this
managers don't know every company in the world So I think it's always important to actually tell them this is like you know fintech

claim_en: Between each job title and its bullet points, add a paragraph explaining what the company is, its sector, how many people the candidate worked with, and the biggest problems faced and how they were fixed, since managers do not know every company.

anchors.quote: We've been doing this so much and managers love this
But that managers really stands out that's incredibly individual to the person

claim_en: Managers love the company paragraph under each job title; it stands out and is incredibly individual to the person.

anchors.quote: have a paragraph three four lines It doesn't have to be long
two three lines it doesn't have to be long some people do very long but I always say too many is a bit difficult to read for managers

claim_en: The company paragraph should be two to four lines; it does not have to be long, and too many lines are difficult for managers to read.

anchors.quote: if it's a startup you know mention that you genuinely worked end to end

claim_en: For a startup role, mention that the candidate genuinely worked end to end.

anchors.quote: if it's a bigger company I think even And then then it's even more important because I think if you put a massive bank it's like okay I've seen the CV before How is this person different to someone else at the bank What problem were they solving How did they go do it

claim_en: At a bigger company, such as a massive bank, it is even more important to say what problem the candidate was solving and how, to show how they differ from others at the same company.

anchors.quote: I've had so many cases where someone messaging the manager directly after applying when they genuinely think I am good for this job
Some people got jobs after it I've seen it so so many times

claim_en: The recruiter has seen many cases where a candidate messaged the hiring manager directly after applying, saying briefly why they fit, and the manager then interviewed them; some got jobs.

anchors.quote: I would send a message and really clearly outline here's why I think I'm good Here's my experience based on the job description It's it's like a cover letter but it's not it's not that long

claim_en: Send the hiring manager a short message that clearly outlines why the candidate fits and their experience against the job description, like a cover letter but shorter.

anchors.quote: what I've seen is a lot of managers care nowadays
now when there's so many people looking they're looking for anything that's extra uh anything that's different
I've seen different ones where people contribute to communities that's brilliant um people want to be seeing that

claim_en: A lot of managers now care about extras: with so many people looking, they look for anything extra or different, such as contributions to communities, which they want to see.

anchors.quote: GitHub's obviously brilliant I always say definitely update it even if you don't put on your CV

claim_en: Keep GitHub updated even when it is not on the CV.

anchors.quote: managers sometimes do go and look for you and try and find your GitHub

claim_en: Managers sometimes look for the candidate and try to find their GitHub even when the CV does not link it.

anchors.quote: So I think definitely if you have something put it in there it won't hurt to have it in there Definitely don't make probably a whole massive part about it but definitely kind of highlight it maybe on the side column and put in bold

claim_en: Asked about coding contest ratings, the recruiter says to put such a rating on the CV if the candidate has one: not as a big part, but highlighted, for example in bold in a side column.
